GEO-A01.title: Two bisectors plus parallels
GEO-A01.recognition: Two angle bisectors inside a parallelogram or between parallel sides usually collapse to one half-angle variable.
GEO-A01.example: In parallelogram ABCD, the bisector of ∠DAB meets BC at M. Suppose another line through D bisects ∠AMC. Show how to reduce all relevant angles to one variable x before using any numerical angle.
steps: Let ∠DAB=2x, so the first bisector gives ∠MAB=x.
Because AD∥BC and AB∥CD, transfer x to the matching angles at M and D; do not create new variables.
Write the full angle ∠AMC as a sum of the transferred pieces. The second bisector now halves a known expression in x.
Only after this reduction should a given numerical angle be substituted.
GEO-A01.legal: Every transferred angle must be justified by one of the two parallelogram parallel pairs.
GEO-A01.wrong: Assigning a different variable at every vertex hides the repeated half-angle structure.
GEO-A01.transfer: If a third line is parallel to AB, which of the x-angles is copied to it?

GEO-A02.title: Line directions in a regular polygon
GEO-A02.recognition: Extended side questions ask for the acute angle between lines, so line direction is modulo 180°.
GEO-A02.example: In a regular 18-gon, compare the lines containing two sides whose directions are separated by four exterior turns. Find their acute line angle.
steps: The exterior turn is 360°/18=20°.
Four turns change the directed side direction by 80°.
As undirected lines, angles are read modulo 180°; 80° is already acute.
Therefore the acute angle between the two side-lines is 80°.
GEO-A02.legal: Count separation in side directions, not in vertex labels alone.
GEO-A02.wrong: Using the interior angle 160° repeatedly produces unnecessary arithmetic.
GEO-A02.transfer: What acute line angle results from five exterior turns in the same 18-gon?

GEO-A03.title: Rectangle area from corner triangles
GEO-A03.recognition: Three known corner-triangle areas around a rectangle often determine the whole area without determining every cut.
GEO-A03.example: A rectangle has width w and height h. E lies on the top edge and F on the right edge. Suppose the three corner triangles have areas 12, 8, and 18. Explain the elimination route to the centre area.
steps: Set T=wh, the whole rectangle area.
If DE=x and BF=y, write the corner areas as hx/2=12, (w-x)(h-y)/2=8, and wy/2=18.
Use hx=24 and wy=36 to replace x and y in the middle equation by expressions involving T.
Solve the resulting equation in T, reject any root smaller than 12+8+18, then subtract the three corner areas from T.
GEO-A03.legal: The selected root must keep E and F on their stated sides and make the centre area positive.
GEO-A03.wrong: Solving x,y,w,h separately creates more unknowns than the problem needs.
GEO-A03.transfer: Why can T never be less than the sum of the three known disjoint corner areas?

GEO-A04.title: Reflection that manufactures a 60° angle
GEO-A04.recognition: If the angle arithmetic naturally produces a 60° gap and you already have equal lengths, a reflection can turn the gap into an equilateral triangle.
GEO-A04.example: Suppose two rays from A differ by 60° after one ray is reflected across a known angle bisector, and the reflected endpoint X satisfies AX=AY. Show what structure is created.
steps: Reflect the original ray across the known bisector; reflection preserves the relevant angle and length.
The reflected ray and the second ray now enclose 60°.
Because AX=AY, triangle AXY is isosceles with vertex angle 60°.
Its base angles are also 60°, so AXY is equilateral; the new 60° and equal-length facts may now be transferred back through the reflection.
GEO-A04.legal: The mirror line must be an actually known line of reflection; do not invent symmetry.
GEO-A04.wrong: Reflecting without a target equality or standard angle usually adds a point but no usable theorem.
GEO-A04.transfer: What changes if the manufactured angle is 90° instead of 60°?

GEO-A05.title: Perpendicular medians with centroid origin
GEO-A05.recognition: Perpendicular medians become perpendicular vertex vectors when the centroid is the origin.
GEO-A05.example: In triangle ABC, the medians from B and C are perpendicular. If AG=8, where G is the centroid, find AB²+BC²+CA².
steps: Put G at the origin and let the vertex vectors be a,b,c. Then a+b+c=0.
The median from B points along -b, and the median from C points along -c, so perpendicular medians give b·c=0.
Since a=-(b+c), |a|²=|b|²+|c|²=64. Thus |a|²+|b|²+|c|²=128.
For centroid origin, AB²+BC²+CA²=3(|a|²+|b|²+|c|²)=384.
GEO-A05.legal: AG is 2/3 of the full A-median, but here AG itself is the given vector length.
GEO-A05.wrong: Using raw coordinates for all three vertices hides the centroid relation a+b+c=0.
GEO-A05.transfer: If AG=10 under the same perpendicular-median condition, how does the final sum scale?

GEO-A06.title: A diameter circle creates altitude feet
GEO-A06.recognition: When a circle has BC as diameter and cuts AB,AC again, Thales turns the new points into feet of altitudes.
GEO-A06.example: In acute triangle ABC, the circle with BC as diameter meets AB again at P and AC again at Q. Prove that CP and BQ are two altitudes of ABC.
steps: Because P is on the diameter circle, ∠BPC=90° by Thales.
P lies on AB, so CP⊥AB; therefore CP is the altitude from C.
Similarly ∠BQC=90° and Q lies on AC, so BQ⊥AC; therefore BQ is the altitude from B.
Their intersection is therefore the orthocenter of ABC.
GEO-A06.legal: The “again” intersections P and Q must lie on the corresponding side-lines; acuteness keeps the usual feet inside the sides.
GEO-A06.wrong: Do not treat P,Q as arbitrary circle points; their side membership is what makes the right angles into altitudes.
GEO-A06.transfer: Which third altitude passes through the intersection of CP and BQ?

GEO-A07.title: Tangent circles on one line
GEO-A07.recognition: Project circle centres to the common tangent line and replace each tangent pair by one horizontal gap.
GEO-A07.example: Two circles of radii 9 and 4 touch each other and the same line. Find the horizontal separation of their centres.
steps: The centre distance is 9+4=13.
Their vertical separation above the line is 9-4=5.
The horizontal separation d satisfies d²+5²=13².
Thus d²=144 and d=12, equivalently d=2√(9·4).
GEO-A07.legal: This formula is for external tangency with both circles tangent to the same line on the same side.
GEO-A07.wrong: Using centre distance r1+r2 as the horizontal gap ignores the different heights of the centres.
GEO-A07.transfer: What is the horizontal gap for radii 16 and 9?

GEO-A08.title: Arc midpoint -> equal chords -> angle bisector
GEO-A08.recognition: A midpoint of arc BC (not containing A) gives equal arcs BD and DC, hence equal chords and equal inscribed angles at A.
GEO-A08.example: In a circle, D is the midpoint of arc BC not containing A. Prove AD bisects ∠BAC.
steps: Arc BD equals arc DC by the definition of arc midpoint.
Equal arcs subtend equal inscribed angles at A: ∠BAD=∠DAC.
Therefore AD bisects ∠BAC.
The same arc equality also gives chord BD=DC, so the midpoint supplies both angular and metric information.
GEO-A08.legal: Specify which arc is bisected; the opposite arc can give a different point.
GEO-A08.wrong: Do not assume D is the midpoint of chord BC; it is the midpoint of an arc.
GEO-A08.transfer: Which two chord lengths become equal automatically?

GEO-A09.title: Homothety plus power at internal tangency
GEO-A09.recognition: Two internally tangent circles give a dilation centred at the tangency point; a tangent from another point supplies a power product.
GEO-A09.example: Two circles of radii 6 and 3 are internally tangent at A. A point P on the larger circle lies on a secant P-A that meets the smaller circle again at B. If AP=8, find the tangent length from P to the smaller circle.
steps: The homothety centred at A has scale 3/6=1/2, so AB/AP=1/2 and AB=4.
Along the secant the order is P-B-A, hence PB=PA-BA=8-4=4.
Power of P with respect to the smaller circle gives PM²=PB·PA=4·8=32.
Thus PM=4√2.
GEO-A09.legal: Use the correct point order on the secant and the whole secant length PA in the power formula.
GEO-A09.wrong: Multiplying PB by BA uses the inside segment instead of the whole secant.
GEO-A09.transfer: If the radius ratio were 2:5, what would replace the factor 1/2?

GEO-A10.title: Two Ptolemy equations and eliminate
GEO-A10.recognition: A moving point on a highly symmetric circumcircle often needs two Ptolemy equations, not one.
GEO-A10.example: Let ABCD be a cyclic rectangle with AB=3, BC=4, AC=BD=5, and let P lie on arc CD. Express BP from quadrilateral A-B-C-P, then write a second Ptolemy equation using B-C-D-P.
steps: For cyclic A-B-C-P, Ptolemy gives AC·BP = AB·CP + BC·AP, hence 5BP=3CP+4AP.
For cyclic B-C-D-P, BD·CP = BC·DP + CD·BP, hence 5CP=4DP+3BP.
The pair is now a linear system in the repeated distances BP and CP.
Depending on the target, add/substitute the two equations to eliminate the unwanted repeated distance.
GEO-A10.legal: Write the vertices in cyclic order in each quadrilateral before choosing diagonals.
GEO-A10.wrong: Applying Ptolemy once may introduce more unknown lengths than it removes.
GEO-A10.transfer: Which repeated distance would you eliminate first if the target involved AP and DP only?

GEO-A11.title: Miquel by “two circles first”
GEO-A11.recognition: Three circles attached to the three sides of a triangle suggest defining the common point from only two circles.
GEO-A11.example: For D∈BC, E∈CA, F∈AB, let M be the second intersection of circles (AEF) and (BFD). Prove the method step that places M on (CDE).
steps: From cyclic A-E-M-F, ∠EMF equals the angle subtending the same chord EF at A, so rewrite it as ∠EAF (using directed angles if extensions occur).
From cyclic B-F-M-D, rewrite ∠FMD as ∠FBD.
Add the two rewritten angles. Because E lies on CA and F on AB, and D lies on BC, the sum matches the angle ∠ECD (up to the same directed-angle convention).
Thus ∠EMD=∠ECD, so C,D,E,M are cyclic and M lies on the third circle.
GEO-A11.legal: When D,E,F are on extensions, directed angles avoid supplementary-angle mistakes.
GEO-A11.wrong: “By Miquel” without constructing M leaves the key execution step unexplained.
GEO-A11.transfer: Which cyclic test could replace the equal-angle test in the last line?

GEO-A12.title: One affine parameter for a moving point
GEO-A12.recognition: A point moving on a segment or mid-segment should usually introduce one parameter, not two coordinates.
GEO-A12.example: Let D,E be fixed points and P move on DE. Write a coordinate-free parameterization and explain how it controls later line intersections.
steps: Choose t with 0≤t≤1 and write P=(1-t)D+tE.
Every coordinate of P is now linear in t. A line through a fixed vertex and P therefore has an equation whose coefficients are linear in t.
Intersecting that line with a fixed side produces a side-division ratio that is a rational function of t.
Keep t symbolic; in invariant problems the final expression often simplifies because the t-dependence cancels.
GEO-A12.legal: Endpoints t=0 or t=1 may create coincident lines; check whether the original problem allows them.
GEO-A12.wrong: Giving P two independent coordinates ignores the fact that P is constrained to one segment.
GEO-A12.transfer: Why is a one-parameter description especially natural when DE is a mid-segment?

GEO-A13.title: Cevian ratios as area weights
GEO-A13.recognition: A point dividing a cevian in a known ratio fixes the area of the opposite small triangle as a fraction of the whole.
GEO-A13.example: Inside triangle ABC, A-P-D with D∈BC and AP:PD=2:1; B-P-E with E∈CA and BP:PE=3:1. Find the fractions [PBC]/[ABC] and [PCA]/[ABC].
steps: Along AD, the perpendicular distance to BC varies linearly from A to 0 at D. Since PD/AD=1/3, [PBC]/[ABC]=1/3.
Along BE, PE/BE=1/4, so [PCA]/[ABC]=1/4.
The remaining area fraction is [PAB]/[ABC]=1-1/3-1/4=5/12.
These three positive fractions can be used as barycentric-style weights without introducing formal barycentric coordinates.
GEO-A13.legal: P must lie inside the triangle for all three ordinary area weights to be positive.
GEO-A13.wrong: Do not confuse AP:PD with the side ratio BD:DC; they are different pieces of data.
GEO-A13.transfer: If CP:PF is known as well, how could you cross-check the three area weights?

GEO-A14.title: Many perpendicularities -> one coordinate axis
GEO-A14.recognition: When several lines are perpendicular, put one important line on the x-axis so each perpendicularity becomes a dot product or zero coordinate.
GEO-A14.example: Take K=(0,0), M=(10,0), N=(10,6). Point L=(2,8) satisfies KL⊥LN. The line through L perpendicular to KN meets KM at O. Find MO.
steps: KN=(10,6), so a perpendicular direction is (6,-10).
The line through L is (x,y)=(2,8)+t(6,-10).
At O on KM, y=0, so 8-10t=0 and t=0.8. Hence O=(6.8,0).
Therefore MO=10-6.8=3.2.
GEO-A14.legal: After solving coordinates, use the stated point order to choose the correct segment length.
GEO-A14.wrong: Slope formulas become fragile for vertical lines; dot products/direction vectors are safer.
GEO-A14.transfer: Check directly that KL·LN=0 in this example.

GEO-A15.title: Equal chord information before median algebra
GEO-A15.recognition: If a median meets the circumcircle again and equal chords appear, use chord geometry before substituting median formulas.
GEO-A15.example: In triangle ABC, the median from A meets the circumcircle again at L. Prove LB=LC if and only if AB=AC.
steps: If LB=LC, point L lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
The median line AL passes through midpoint M of BC, so line LM is the perpendicular bisector; hence AM⊥BC.
A median that is also an altitude makes right triangles ABM and ACM congruent, so AB=AC.
Conversely, if AB=AC, the median AM is also the perpendicular bisector of BC; since L lies on AM, LB=LC.
GEO-A15.legal: Use the fact that the median line passes through the midpoint of BC; equal chords alone do not identify a median.
GEO-A15.wrong: Jumping directly to Apollonius misses the stronger circle symmetry.
GEO-A15.transfer: What equal-angle statement on the circumcircle is equivalent to LB=LC?

GEO-A16.title: Propagate through a chain of isosceles triangles
GEO-A16.recognition: Consecutive equal segments create overlapping isosceles triangles; start from the end with a fixed angle and work inward.
GEO-A16.example: Points A,B,D are collinear. Suppose AB=BC=CD and ∠BDC=40°. Find ∠BAC.
steps: BC=CD, so triangle BCD is isosceles and ∠CBD=∠BDC=40°.
Because BA and BD are opposite rays, ∠ABC=180°-40°=140°.
AB=BC, so triangle ABC is isosceles with equal base angles at A and C.
Thus each base angle is (180°-140°)/2=20°, so ∠BAC=20°.
GEO-A16.legal: The straight-line supplement at B depends on the stated collinearity and point order.
GEO-A16.wrong: Introducing a new variable in every small triangle is slower than propagating fixed angles.
GEO-A16.transfer: If ∠BDC were 35°, what changes in the final base-angle calculation?
